stop1.p1: Kaspa is digital cash secured by proof of work, like Bitcoin — but built to be fast.
stop1.p2: Most blockchains make one block at a time and throw away ties. Kaspa keeps every block and weaves them into a blockDAG — a braid instead of a single chain — ordered by a protocol called GHOSTDAG. The practical result: blocks arrive many times per second and payments confirm in seconds, while keeping Bitcoin-style proof-of-work security.
stop1.quote: A chain is a single-lane road; a blockDAG is a motorway where every lane's traffic still ends up in one agreed order.
stop1.p3: For years Kaspa's scripting was deliberately minimal. It could verify who owns coins and move them, but it couldn't enforce conditions on how coins move next. No vaults, no chain-enforced tokens, no on-chain agreements — money only.
stop1.p4: That is what the Toccata upgrade changed, and it's why this site exists.

stop2.p1: Toccata is the 2026 upgrade that taught Kaspa to enforce rules on money, not just move it. Before it, the chain could answer one question: "does this signature match?" After it, the chain can check a whole contract's worth of conditions before letting coins move.
afterItems: Covenants — rules attached to coins that every future spend must satisfy
Chain-enforced tokens — the KCC-20 approach: supply and transfer rules checked by consensus itself
Inline zero-knowledge verification — the chain can check a cryptographic proof that something happened, without seeing the details
words: Covenant — a lock on coins that dictates how they're allowed to move next. Not advice, not a bookkeeper's note: consensus rejects any spend that breaks it.
Lineage (KIP-17) — a covenant can prove where its coins came from, so rules can follow coins across many transactions.
Covenant ID (KIP-20) — a stable identity for a covenant, so one contract can own things and be found again.
Inline ZK (KIP-16) — zero-knowledge proof checking, live on mainnet since 2026-06-30.
stop2.quote: Before Toccata, Kaspa was a very fast cash register. After Toccata, it's a cash register that can also hold escrow, run a vault, and issue tokens — with the rules built into the machine.

stop3.lede: Bottom to top: each layer exists to make the one below it usable. One sentence, one analogy, and an honest maturity badge each.

kaspa-script.name: Kaspa Script + Covenants++
kaspa-script.plain: Rules built into the money itself. A covenant is a lock on coins that says exactly how they are allowed to move next — and the chain refuses any spend that breaks the rule.
kaspa-script.analogy: The vault door: the combination logic is machined into the door itself, not written on a sign next to it.

silverscript.name: Silverscript
silverscript.plain: A language for writing rules the chain itself enforces — without wiring the raw script by hand. You describe the allowed state changes; the compiler produces the covenant.
silverscript.analogy: Writing the combination logic for the vault door — without machining the door yourself.

argent.name: Argent
argent.plain: An app framework one level up: instead of one contract, you write actors — separate covenants that talk to each other — and Argent compiles the whole app down through Silverscript.
argent.analogy: Many vault doors that work together: each actor is a door, and Argent wires the corridors between them.

kcc-20.name: KCC-20
kcc-20.plain: Tokens built as covenants, so supply and transfer rules are checked by Kaspa consensus itself — no off-chain bookkeeper has to be trusted. Live and traded on mainnet; the written standard is a draft still being consolidated, with no tagged release yet.
kcc-20.analogy: Tokens whose rulebook is machined into the vault door — nobody outside the chain keeps the score.

vprogs.name: vProgs / CDAG
vprogs.plain: Programs that live natively inside Kaspa's DAG rather than being encoded as covenant scripts. The kaspanet/vprogs repo is public — a Rust framework for provable computation, in early development. Not something you can deploy on mainnet today.
vprogs.analogy: Blueprints for a smarter vault — now pinned up in a public workshop, but the vault isn't built yet.

stop4.lede: One story, top of the stack to the bottom: a vault that protects coins even from a thief holding your keys. Every layer you met at the last stop does one job here.

steps.title: Start with a rule worth enforcing
steps.body: "These coins can only be withdrawn after a 24-hour delay, and only to my address — no matter who steals my keys tonight." That sentence is a vault.

steps.title: Write the rule as code
steps.body: A few dozen lines describing the allowed state changes: old state + your request + the transaction's facts → the new state that's permitted. Nothing else is.

steps.title: The compiler machines the lock
steps.body: Silverscript compiles your rule down to Kaspa Script — the raw covenant the chain understands. You never hand-wire this layer, the compiler does.

steps.title: Deposit — the rule becomes physics
steps.body: You send coins into the covenant. From this moment the rule isn't a promise or a company policy: every node on the network checks it on every spend attempt.

steps.title: A thief tries — and the chain says no
steps.body: Someone with your stolen keys broadcasts an instant withdrawal. The spend breaks the delay rule, so consensus rejects the transaction like a coin that doesn't fit the slot. It never happened.

steps.title: Anyone can verify it
steps.body: The covenant, its rules and its history are public. An explorer like kascov.io shows the vault sitting there, enforcing itself, with no company in the loop.

stop4.note: Multi-contract apps follow the same story with one extra chapter: Argent wires several covenants into one application before everything compiles down.

stop5.lede: This is the real SimpleCovenant from the official tutorial — the same twelve lines this site compiles in CI every day. Imagine coins locked by it, with the recipient baked in at creation being you. Play the thief. Press the buttons.
stop5.simNote: This lesson runs in your browser against the contract's logic — no coins move. Every verdict shows the rule a real node would apply. Live testnet-10 broadcast: coming.
stop5.attemptsLabel: Build a spend and submit it

attempts.steal: 🦹 Thief: send the coins to the thief's address
attempts.stealhome: 🦹 Thief: send the coins to your address
attempts.split: 🤔 Thief: output 0 to you… plus an output 1 to the thief

stop5.passVerdict: ✓ PASSES — the rule allows this spend
stop5.failVerdict: ✗ FAILS — the rule this spend breaks is highlighted

lessons.steal: This spend breaks the rule — require() fails, so on chain it would never become a transaction at all. Even with your keys stolen, the thief could not move these coins anywhere but your address: the rule is in the coin, not in a server.
lessons.stealhome: ACCEPTED — the thief just spent your vault… straight into your pocket. Read the contract again: it never checks who signs. It checks where the money goes. The rule is the lock, not the key.
lessons.honest: ACCEPTED — the ordinary path. The same rule that blocked the thief lets you through, because the rule only ever cared about the destination.
lessons.split: ACCEPTED — you found the hole. Nothing here constrains amounts or other outputs, so a tutorial contract makes a terrible vault. The chain enforced exactly what was written; the writing was the weakness. This is why production covenants pin amounts and outputs — and why audits matter.

items.q: Is this like Ethereum smart contracts?
items.a: Same goal — programmable rules on-chain — different shape. Ethereum runs programs against big shared account balances. Kaspa covenants attach rules directly to specific coins (UTXOs): smaller and stricter per contract, but the rules travel with the money itself and inherit Kaspa's speed and proof-of-work security.

items.q: Do I need to understand covenants to hold KAS?
items.a: No. Plain sending and receiving is unchanged. The stack matters when you want more than transfer: vaults, escrow, tokens with chain-enforced rules — or when you want to judge a project that claims to use them.

As of this site's last review: Silverscript hit v1.0.0 on 2026-09-09 but names no external audit and its own security policy still calls it experimental. Argent has no tagged release at all. The status board tracks this daily — and any project's "audited" claim deserves a named auditor and a date before you believe it.

items.q: What is KCC-20, in one line?
items.a: Tokens whose supply and transfer rules are checked by Kaspa consensus itself — no off-chain bookkeeper to trust. They are live and traded on mainnet while the written standard is still being consolidated.

items.q: What are vProgs, and can I use them?
items.a: Not yet — vProgs (native programs living in the DAG) are the research track, the roadmap beyond covenants. Anyone selling you a "vProg" today is early by definition.

items.q: Where would I actually start building?
items.a: Kascov.io lets you try covenant code with zero installation, and Silverscript is the language most things are written in today. The Build section walks the whole path: toolchain, a first 12-line covenant, testnet, and the examples worth reading.

faq.finishP: You now know more about Kaspa's programmability stack than most of crypto Twitter. options: A braid of parallel blocks that are all kept and put in one agreed order
A chain that throws away blocks which arrive at the same time
A database maintained by the Kaspa foundation
kaspa-in-60-seconds.why: Kaspa keeps every block and lets GHOSTDAG order them — that's why it can run many blocks per second without giving up proof-of-work security.

kaspa-in-60-seconds.q: Before the Toccata upgrade, Kaspa could…
options: verify signatures and move coins — money only
kaspa-in-60-seconds.why: Kaspa's scripting was deliberately minimal: it verified who owns coins and moved them. Conditions on how coins move next came with Toccata.

options: A promise a project makes in its whitepaper
An entry in an indexer's database
A rule attached to coins that consensus itself enforces
what-toccata-changed.why: Not advice, not bookkeeping: any spend that breaks the rule is rejected by every node. The rule travels with the money.

what-toccata-changed.q: A spend that breaks a covenant rule is…
options: not a transaction at all — consensus rejects it
what-toccata-changed.why: There is no appeal process because there is nothing to appeal — the network treats it like a coin that doesn't fit the slot.

what-toccata-changed.q: Inline ZK verification (KIP-16) lets the chain…
options: check a cryptographic proof that something happened, without seeing the details
what-toccata-changed.why: A covenant can require a valid zero-knowledge proof before coins move — live on mainnet since 2026-06-30.

meet-the-stack.why: You describe the allowed state changes; the compiler produces the covenant the chain understands. You never wire the raw script by hand.

meet-the-stack.q: Argent is the right layer when…
options: you want a token counted by indexers
several contracts must act together atomically
meet-the-stack.why: Actors + ICC exist exactly for multi-contract apps. One contract alone is Silverscript territory — and Argent has no tagged release yet.

options: a research roadmap — nothing to build with yet
meet-the-stack.why: Native DAG programs are the research track beyond covenants. Anyone selling you a vProg today is early by definition.

how-it-fits-together.q: After you deposit into a covenant vault, who checks the rule?
options: Every node on the network, on every spend attempt
how-it-fits-together.why: That's the whole point: the rule stops being a policy and becomes physics — no company in the loop.

how-it-fits-together.q: A thief who steals your keys can…
options: only move the coins where the covenant rule allows
how-it-fits-together.why: The rule is the lock, not the key. You can press this button yourself on the next stop of the tour.
